cards.explanation: The answer is to pass it down, generation after generation. Joel says, “Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation.” That's a story with a long road ahead of it. I can barely get a cookie recipe through one retelling before somebody swaps out the sprinkles. He's speaking to the elders and everyone in the land, so the whole land is in on this.

The answer is True. Joel lines the locusts up one by one. What the devouring locust left, the swarming locust ate. What the swarming locust left, the young locust ate, and what the young locust left, the destroying locust ate. It's like four people going through a cookie box in a row, and the last one is down on his knees hunting crumbs.

The answer is that the sweet wine is cut off from them. Joel says to “wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it has been cut off from your mouth.” The text names that loss as the reason and nothing else. I think this one stings for them.

The answer is that it splinters the fig tree. Joel says this nation “…has laid waste My grapevine and splintered My fig tree.” Then it strips off the bark and throws it away, and the branches turn white. Splintered means broken into pieces, friends. Nobody was gentle about it.

The answer is grain. Joel says, “Grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD…” So the loss isn't only talked about in the fields. Verse 13 speaks of the grain and drink offerings again, as withheld from the house of your God.

The answer is False, and it's a sad picture. The priests are not rejoicing. Joel says, “the priests are in mourning, those who minister before the LORD.” The grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD. I think this is one of the quieter, heavier parts of the passage.

The answer is the farmers and the vinedressers. Joel says, “Be dismayed, O farmers, wail, O vinedressers, over the wheat and barley…” Those are the two groups he names. The reason he gives is that the harvest of the field has perished.

The answer is joy. Joel says, “Surely the joy of mankind has dried up.” That comes right after he names the grapevine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, the palm and the apple, all withered. He says all the trees of the orchard are withered. I've seen what happens to a bakery with no flour. Nobody's laughing.

The answer is through the night. Joel says, “Come, spend the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God…” The time he names is the night. He's speaking to the ministers of the altar. The grain and drink offerings are withheld from the house of their God.

The answer is the elders. Joel says, “Gather the elders and all the residents of the land to the house of the LORD your God…” He spoke to the elders back in verse 2 as well. The call goes out to all the residents of the land too, and it names the house of the LORD as the place.

The answer is to cry out to the LORD. Joel says to gather them at the house of the LORD “…and cry out to the LORD.” That's the instruction he gives for the gathering. Crying out to Him is what he says to do. Sometimes that's the whole bake, friends.

The answer is False. Joel says, “Alas for the day! For the Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.” He says near, not far off. It's a heavy moment, and Joel doesn't soften it.

The answer is destruction. Joel says, “…it will come as destruction from the Almighty.” He says it right after “Alas for the day!” and just before that he says the Day of the LORD is near. I think this is one of the most serious lines in the passage.

The answer is that the grain has withered away. Joel says, “the storehouses are in ruins; the granaries are broken down, for the grain has withered away.” A granary is where the grain is kept, and the grain is gone. A storage building with nothing to store is a pretty sad building. Think of an empty cookie jar, only a whole lot bigger.

The answer is that they have no pasture. Joel says, “How the cattle groan! The herds wander in confusion because they have no pasture.” The text gives that as the reason. Even the flocks of sheep are suffering.

The answer is fire. The prayer says, “To You, O LORD, I call, for fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field.” That's fire and flames, both in one verse. It's a hard picture, and the prayer takes it straight to the LORD. That's where it goes.

The answer is the beasts of the field. The passage says, “Even the beasts of the field pant for You, for the streams of water have dried up…” So the animals are named too, panting for Him. The streams of water have dried up. I think that's one of the most tender lines in the whole passage.
